text: Flattery dies somewhere between your chest and your mouth. Venus, the part of you that likes, praises, and takes pleasure, sits on Aldebaran, the bright eye of the Bull in the constellation Taurus, a star that has never tolerated the decorative version of anything. So your warmth ignites only for the genuine article. Politeness you can produce on demand, but enthusiasm refuses to be manufactured in you, and the difference shows: the voice flattens, the compliment lands one beat late, and the person collecting it usually notices. There are social costs. Plenty of rooms run on pleasant insincerity, and you stand in them like someone unable to make change in the local currency. What you get back is a kind of credit rating. Praise that cannot be bought or hurried holds its value, so people keep the good thing you said about their work for years, repeat it to themselves in low moments, and build on it, knowing it was weighed before it left you. Your taste holds to the same standard. You want honest materials, things that are what they claim: solid wood over veneer, the plain true sentence over the ornamented one, the friend who names the price up front. Affection from you arrives with its terms visible, which blunt people find abrupt and tired people find restful. The craft to learn is timing rather than softening. Your true reading of the draft, the plan, the room, offered while the stakes are still small, costs a wince and spares a disaster; the same reading held in until it bursts out arrives with interest added. Nothing here asks you to become a flatterer. Deliver the honesty earlier, and it does its work while the work can still be changed.

Your liking behaves like patronage. With Venus on Regulus, the royal star at the heart of the Lion in the constellation Leo, favor is never a passive feeling in you: when you decide that a person, a small shop, a half-built project is good, you seat it at your table, lend it your name, and argue its case in rooms it cannot enter yet. More than a few ventures around you carry an early boost from your regard the way plants carry weather. Your taste has the same royal grain. You would rather own one excellent thing than five adequate ones, hospitality feels to you like a form of honor, and shabbiness in your surroundings wears on you faster than it wears on most people. The tangle sits where regard meets admiration. Warmth flows out of you most easily toward people at their best, the friend mid-triumph, the artist in form, and when someone you love goes gray for a season, dull, struggling, hard to be proud of, your affection can turn formal at exactly the hour it was needed plain. That is not disloyalty. It is an aesthetic reflex, the eye flinching from decline, and you can override it once you have caught it operating. The override is simple to describe: love first, admire second, and let the order show. Sit with the friend whose project failed without redecorating the failure. Keep the same chair at your table for someone who currently brings nothing to it. What comes back is worth the discomfort. The people you keep through their unimpressive seasons become the company you trust most, because whatever holds you together has stopped depending on either of you performing well.

Pleasant is not the same as alive, and you can taste the difference from across a room. Venus on Antares, the red star burning at the heart of the Scorpion in the constellation Scorpius, gives your capacity for pleasure and attachment no middle register worth speaking of. What draws you is the real thing at full strength: the talk that finally gets past the weather, the meal worth silence, the piece of music you have to stop walking for, the person who says what they mean on the first pass. Mild amusements slide off you. A curated, agreeable evening can leave you strangely tired, while one honest hour leaves you fed for a week, and you have probably rearranged parts of your life around that arithmetic without ever naming it. Named, it becomes easier to run. The old warnings about this star describe wreckage; the actual distortion is narrower. In you, calm can be misread as cooling. When a bond settles into peace, the appetite that only registers full strength may report that nothing is happening, and you can find yourself picking at the seams, opening the sharp topic at midnight, testing whether the wiring is still live. Sometimes it does need testing. More often the quiet was only quiet, the steady burn of a thing that has stopped needing to prove itself, and the test is what leaves the scorch marks. The discernment this contact asks you to build is between missing the person and missing the voltage. From inside they feel identical, and they are not. A useful check when the itch arrives: wait a day, then see whether what you wanted was the person or the jolt. Real closeness produces its own storms on an honest schedule; nothing requires you to schedule extras. A bond that has already survived your scrutiny earns some seasons in which you decline, on purpose, to scrutinize it.

What you fall for is rarely only the thing in front of you. Venus on Fomalhaut, the solitary bright star at the mouth of the Southern Fish, the constellation Piscis Austrinus, gives your taste a horizon: the song matters for the country it implies, the room pleases because of the life that could be lived in it, and the objects you keep longest are the ones that point past themselves. Shopping with you is a strange errand. You are not acquiring items, you are collecting evidence of a world you half remember. The same lens turns on people. You perceive the finest version of a person, the one they have not become yet, and your regard addresses that version directly. Being seen that way is powerful, and more than one person has grown into a self your attention drafted first. But the person at the sink is not the figure in the vision, and on a flat afternoon you can find yourself tender toward what someone could be while going vague toward who they are, which the actual person feels as a draft under the door. The ideal is not the enemy, and nobody should ask you to want ordinary things in an ordinary way. The correction is smaller: aim the reverence at what is actually present. The specific laugh, the particular hands, the exact stubbornness, studied closely, turn out to be stranger and finer than the projected version anyway; reality outperforms the brochure whenever you give it the same quality of attention. Loyalty built on the observed person survives weather that loyalty to a vision does not. You will keep hearing the far signal your whole life, and it does not need silencing. Let it tune you toward the people beside you rather than past them, and the beauty you keep sensing at a distance starts turning up at close range.

Some of what you want, you learned early to keep off the record. Venus on Algol sets your tastes and attractions on the most notorious star in Perseus, the one the old charts drew as a blinking demon eye, and for centuries astrologers told scare stories about exactly this pairing. Strip off the horror varnish and what remains is appetite with real weight behind it. When you want something, you want it with your whole chest: the person, the dessert, the velvet coat, the hour of doing absolutely nothing. There is no irony in your liking and no committee in your choosing, and people around you learn to trust your yes because they have seen the shape of your no. The trouble the old stories point at begins with concealment, not with the wanting. Somewhere along the way, many carriers of this contact absorbed the idea that their appetite was too much, and started editing: the enthusiasm understated, the desire mentioned only as a joke, the want starved in public and fed in secret. A want managed that way does not shrink. It grows a private life, and private lives negotiate poorly on your behalf. The repair is admission before negotiation. Not every want gets granted; every want gets a hearing, in plain words, in daylight, before it has time to go quiet and strange. Say the true size of an appetite to one person who can hear it without ceremony, and notice that nothing catches fire. A desire you have already admitted cannot ambush you, and ambush is most of what the old books were actually afraid of.

Certain kinds of beauty tighten your throat, and not exactly from sadness. With Venus on Alcyone, brightest of the Pleiades, the small clustered sisters riding the Bull's shoulder, your sense of pleasure is tuned to the transient: late light on a wall, the closing night of something good, the song that knows it is about time passing. Delight arrives in you with an ache alloyed into it, and the ache is not a flaw in the enjoyment; it is the depth of it. You love things partly because they will not last, and that awareness gives your attention a quality other people can feel, a way of being fully inside an evening because you register, even mid-laughter, that it is already leaving. Affection follows the same tuning. You hold your people a little the way you would hold them at a departure gate, and your tenderness has an unusual completeness because of it; nothing about anyone you love goes unnoticed for long. Trouble starts only when the elegy runs ahead of the event. You can spend a golden hour rehearsing its loss instead of having it, mourning a summer in June, grieving a friendship that is sitting right there asking what you want to do this weekend. When you notice the rehearsal starting, come back to the hour it is borrowing from. The endings need no advance work from you; they manage their own arrivals. The sweetness is the part that needs you present, and staying present to it is the thing you were built to do unusually well.

You have never once liked something quietly. Venus on Sirius sets the affections on the brightest star in the night sky, the great dog of Canis Major, and they shine accordingly: your enthusiasms carry, your praise travels, and the small place you love tends to end up with a line out the door partly because you could not stop telling people. Loving, in you, is close kin to celebrating. The gift runs a size too large, the toast gets made, the person you are proud of gets shown to the whole table, and none of it is staged; the wattage is simply native. There is a guardian under the shine as well, the dog being a faithful animal. Your devotion, once given, patrols, and people inside it get defended in rooms they never enter. Where this wants skill is the fit between the celebration and its recipient. Some people bloom under the full beam; others squint. The friend who dreads their own birthday, the quiet one whose promotion you announced before they had told their family, the person who wanted the small dinner and got the crowd: each was loved sincerely and lit wrong. The remedy is not dimming, which would cost you something real, but aiming. Learning each person's actual size of occasion, and matching it, turns out to be a more intimate act than any amount of brightness. Ask first, once, quietly. The question tells the person more about your affection than the fireworks would have, and it costs you nothing but the surprise.

Being liked has never been your project. It simply happens, the way weather happens, because Venus in your chart sits on Spica, the ear of wheat in the Virgin's hand, in the constellation Virgo, the one famous star with no dark chapter in its file. Friendship finds you without campaigns. Invitations arrive, your taste gets trusted and borrowed, and the small social fumbles that would dog anyone else evaporate by morning. Enjoy all of that; it is real, and it is not going anywhere. The gap it leaves is specific: what never breaks never teaches mending. Bonds that maintain themselves give you no practice at repair, so the rare genuine rupture, when one finally reaches you, can find you strangely unequipped, convinced somewhere below argument that conflict and ending are the same event. They are not, but you may be years behind on coursework everyone else was forced through young. The way to catch up is to stop charming past the small frictions. Take the minor disagreement instead of dissolving it. Say the slightly uncomfortable sentence while it is still minor. Let one low-stakes argument run its whole course to the far side, and notice that the far side exists. What you learn there is the one thing the ease could never teach you: a mended bond holds differently from an untested one, and your hands can be trusted with the needle.

You liked it before it was anything. That is the signature of Venus on Arcturus, the golden star of the Herdsman, Bootes, who walks ahead of what he keeps: your regard runs in front of the consensus. The musician with forty listeners, the neighborhood no one's cousin would visit yet, the newcomer whose worth nobody has priced, the awkward early version of a thing that later becomes obvious: your affection finds them first, and your backing is often the first real backing they get. Loving early is a form of scouting, and you are good at the whole craft of it, including the unglamorous stretch where you defend the choice for years before anyone agrees. Watch what happens in you at the moment the crowd shows up, though. When the band fills theaters and the neighborhood gets its magazine feature, something in you quietly starts packing, and loving-first can turn into loving-only-while-first without your ever deciding it. Some of that is honest taste; things do get worse when they scale. Some of it is the discovery premium wearing off, and the difference matters, because walking away at the point of arrival abandons things at exactly the hour your loyalty would mean most and cost least. The sorting question is plain: did the thing change, or did the company? When the answer is the company, stay. Keep a few early loves for the long haul, on purpose, straight past fashionable and out the far side, and you get a pleasure the scouting never supplies: knowing a thing in every season it has had, which no latecomer, however sincere, can buy back.

You court everything a little. Dinner for one gets a set table, the borrowed book goes home wrapped, the throwaway email carries one turned phrase: with Venus on Vega, the anchor star of the small harp Lyra, pleasure is something you compose rather than merely have. The tradition attached music and refinement to this star wherever it touches, and on the planet of affection it makes an artist of the occasion. You know how celebration works, how a room wants arranging, which gift a particular person has been not quite saying they wanted, and the people in your life accumulate a private museum of moments you made beautiful on purpose. None of this is performance in the hollow sense. Form is your sincerity; making it lovely is how you say it mattered. The strain arrives in the long unarranged middle of any real attachment, because bonds have stretches that resist composition: the paperwork years, the sickroom, the four hundredth identical breakfast, the seasons when nothing is an occasion and nobody claps. When there is nothing to arrange, your attention can quietly slacken, and you can mistake the end of the courtship for the end of the feeling, when all that actually ended was the part with your instrument in it. The deeper craft, the one this contact spends a lifetime teaching, is composition at kitchen scale. The ordinary Tuesday given five degrees more care than it strictly needed. The dull errand run as a small ceremony for two. The plain week left plain but fully inhabited, the way a rest is still part of the score. Your gift was never only the flowers or the phrasing. It is the conviction that love should be made well, and the plain stretches are not exempt from that conviction; they are where it does its finest work unwitnessed.

Your address book has no theme. The colleague from two jobs ago, the ceramicist met in a queue, a neighbor's visiting parent, the friend who only exists on long walks: Venus on Capella, the little she-goat riding the Charioteer's shoulder in the constellation Auriga, collects people the way travelers collect towns, one genuine curiosity at a time. Liking, for you, begins as interest. You want to know how a person works, what they have seen, what it is like to be them on a weekday, and affection follows the questions in. Your taste keeps the same open borders: the unfamiliar cuisine ordered without ceremony, the art form you knew nothing about last year, the enthusiasm happily borrowed from whoever is sitting next to you. And your terms run on a long leash in both directions. You do not grip, you do not care to be gripped, friendships in your keeping survive two years of silence and resume mid-sentence, and half the introductions that changed other people's lives got made at your table without your keeping count. Breadth can spread thin, though, and a hold as light as yours reads as low stakes to someone who needed to matter more than averagely; a few people will always ask of you a weight you were not planning to set down anywhere. The more interesting frontier is inward, and it is easy for you to miss because it does not look like new territory. The person you have known for ten years is not finished. They have changed three times since you last asked them the traveler's questions, the ones you save for strangers, and asking again costs nothing but the assumption that you already know them. Depth, approached your way, is simply travel in a country that keeps reissuing visas, and the tenth year of a friendship turns out to hold country the first year never mentioned.

A well-made thing can stop you in the street. The dovetail joint, the honest seam, the sentence with nothing wasted, the small tool that fits the hand as if grown there: with Venus on Rigel, the bright forward foot of Orion, your sense of beauty and your sense of function are a single judgment. Ornament that does no work leaves you cold, and no amount of styling redeems an object that wobbles. The same eye chooses your company. Competence, for you, sits close to courtship: someone wholly absorbed in work they are good at, hands sure, attention gathered, draws you more than any arranged charm, and you have probably loved a few skills as much as you loved their owners. It is a fine way to be drawn to the world, and it carries one rough edge worth sanding. Regard that indexes to competence quietly grades everyone in reach. Your interest can sag when someone is clumsy at their own thing, your patience shortens around a fumbled task, and people close to you can end up feeling reviewed when all they wanted was company. The grading does not spare you either. So the skill this contact actually asks you to acquire is idleness in good company: the afternoon that builds nothing, the conversation with no output, liking someone while they are being useless and letting yourself be liked while you are. Nothing has to come to a point. Some of the strongest joinery in your life gets made in exactly those unproductive hours, by no visible workmanship at all.

Enjoyment has never needed to be earned in your house. Venus on Betelgeuse, the red giant glowing on the raised shoulder of Orion, brings the sky's most generous case file to the pleasures: you eat the good bread while it is warm, take the nap without holding a hearing, accept the compliment without auditing it for motive. Guilt, the standard tax on delight, mostly fails to find you. Around someone like this, other people's shoulders drop. You give whole rooms permission to enjoy themselves simply by visibly doing it first, and your praise, which costs you nothing, gets handed out freely and warms more than you know. Ease that always arrived on its own is easy to file as weather, though, when a good deal of it is actually gifts with senders: the friend who always books the table, the one who remembers what you like before you say it, the standing warmth several people quietly maintain in your direction. Weather needs no thanks. Senders do. The correction costs a sentence here and there. Name what someone did, to them, while it is fresh. Return the specific favor rather than the general goodwill. Once in a while, be the one who books the table and remembers the dish. Gratitude spoken while things are still good is rare enough that people keep it for years, and it spends the one currency this contact handed you in surplus.

The night before the trip may be your favorite part of the trip. Venus on Procyon, the small bright star of Canis Minor that rises just ahead of the great dog star, puts your capacity for delight out in front of events: you savor in advance. The menu gets read online days early, the ticket sits on the fridge quietly glowing, and the plan for a party hands you two weeks of pleasure before a single guest arrives. This is not impatience. Anticipation, in you, is a full-bodied pleasure in its own right, possibly the keenest one you have, and a calendar with nothing coming up starves you faster than an empty pantry would. The event itself, though, can land as a slight comedown, the actual evening thinner than its overture, and you may catch yourself already savoring the next thing while the current one is still on the table. So plant the future on purpose: keep something real to look forward to at all times, and let small things count, since this is fuel rather than frivolity. Then, when the awaited hour arrives, treat arrival as its own discipline: phone away, eyes up, the attention you gave the approach aimed now at the thing itself. Practiced, that turns the comedown into a second helping, the same evening enjoyed once in advance and once in the room.

Nobody guesses your favorites. Venus on Scheat, the star holding a corner of the Great Square of Pegasus, cuts your taste from cloth the common catalogue does not stock: the record almost nobody else plays, the beauty in things politely filed under odd, pleasures with no section in the magazine. Affection runs the same way. The forms of closeness that actually suit you, the odd hours, the particular distances, the devotions shaped like nothing in the manual everyone else seemed to receive, were never listed anywhere, and somewhere early you may have started pre-apologizing for all of it, converting your real enthusiasms into acceptable ones before letting them out of the house. The conversion is the only real problem here. The taste itself needs no correcting; the catalogue was simply written by other people, about other people. What comes back when you stop converting is easy to underestimate. Answer honestly, once, when someone asks what you love, and notice how little goes wrong. Most people turn out to be hungrier for a real enthusiasm than for an approved one, and the evenings when you offered yours uncut are probably already the ones you remember best.
